rv.q: What makes this theatrical enterprise so compelling is the way it transforms what could be dusty historical pageantry into intimate, immediate drama.
The RSC's magnificent adaptation of Hilary Mantel's novels about Thomas Cromwell arrives on Broadway with most of its power intact, offering a masterclass in ensemble acting.
As a fast-paced political thriller, it is fiendishly engaging, and director Jeremy Herrin's 23-member corps skillfully slips in and out of multiple roles.
Of course, those fits of pique can land people in the Tower, a sobering reality that closes this absorbing, uncommonly ambitious chronicle on a chilling note.
There's nothing bookish about the highly theatrical approach taken in director Jeremy Herrin's lucidly told, handsomely staged and emotionally charged production.
Being fun in period costume for nearly five-and-a-half hours of live theater is no mean achievement.
The stage production is more of a pageant, visually beautiful but a little flat.
It is hard not to wish for something deeper from all those hours onstage.
Wolf Hall still feels incomplete. Because it is.
As well-acted, grandly staged and beautifully lit as it is, the show still manages to be tedious.
Mr. Poulton's 51/2-hour stage version of 'Wolf Hall,' unlike Bolt's immaculately crafted, endlessly quotable play, is competent but dullish, a procession of short, ...
This is a magnificent evening in the theater that brings history to life with intelligence, wit and dramatic power that will leave you breathless.
The immensely talented actors manage to make every backroom deal, courtier spat, and royal tantrum fully enjoyable.
The show is shot through with sly parries and juicy jabs.
Lydia Leonard is positively electric as the king's second wife.

Miles closely resembles Robert Stack in that vintage TV series “The Untouchables”: He maintains an implacable façade regardless of what he’s thinking, and that Miles rivets our attention for six hours makes his performance a masterclass in minimalist acting.
The supple performances provided by these and other cast members cannot, however, compensate for plays that impress but don't transport us.
But is it the subtle, engrossing, mysterious masterpiece that Mantel's novels deserved?
"Wolf Hall" is a stiff, step-by-step, plodding march through English history, leaving little space for character development.
But some adaptations simply work better than others.

cn.t: The RSC's epic six-hour adaptation earns praise for its ensemble acting and theatrical craft, transforming Tudor history into compelling drama, though some critics find the lengthy production plodding and dull despite its intrigue-filled subject matter.

vs.sum: The Winter Garden Theatre offers excellent legroom and spacious seating, making it one of the most comfortable venues on Broadway. Sightlines are generally good, though some side seats may have partial obstructions. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historical charm and garden-themed decor, while facilities are average with some potential for lines at restrooms.

acc.note: 20 wheelchair spaces (largest of Shubert theaters). 16 aisle transfer seats. Infrared devices available.
